## Statement

Identifying a sustained-strategy effect requires consistency, sequential exchangeability and positivity, and the estimator families differ in which nuisance components they need. When those components are fitted by machine learning, the model that predicts treatment best is not the model that minimizes the finite-sample error of the causal estimator: a highly adaptive learner can achieve excellent discrimination while returning near-zero treatment probabilities, poor longitudinal balance and invalid inference. Balance-calibrated weight fitting exists and has been applied, so the field is not selecting on prediction alone. What is missing is a criterion that combines predictive risk with the estimator-specific diagnostics that matter, longitudinal balance, weight tails and the remainder-rate condition, in one selection rule, and a default library tuned that way rather than for prediction.

## Why it is open

The causal loss is not computable the way a predictive loss is, because the contrast being targeted is never observed, so the quantity one would cross-validate against does not exist as a label. Balance and weight-dispersion criteria are computable and are not losses in the decision-theoretic sense, and a learner can optimize them while fitting poorly. Which diagnostics apply depends on the estimator, so a single universal criterion is the wrong object and a family of estimator-specific ones has to be built and validated separately.

## What has been tried

::: {.table-scroll}

| Work | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| [Robins JM, Hernán MA, Brumback B. Marginal structural models and causal inference in epidemiology. Epidemiology 2000;11(5):550-560](https://doi.org/10.1097/00001648-200009000-00011) | Introduces marginal structural models and inverse probability weighting for time-varying confounding affected by prior treatment. The nuisance models are parametric and their selection is not addressed. |
| [Feuerriegel S, Frauen D, Melnychuk V, et al. Causal machine learning for predicting treatment outcomes. Nat Med 2024;30:958-968](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-024-02902-1) | Sets out what causal machine learning can and cannot do, and states that individualized effect estimation rests on the same identification assumptions as conventional methods. |
| [ltmle: Longitudinal Targeted Maximum Likelihood Estimation. CRAN](https://cran.r-project.org/package=ltmle) | Implements longitudinal TMLE, IPTW and g-computation, and accepts a SuperLearner library whose selection is left to the analyst. |

:::

## Probable solution or research direction

Construct selection rules that combine predictive risk with longitudinal standardized differences, weight-tail behavior and an estimate of the influence-function remainder, specified per estimator rather than universally, and test whether they select models with lower causal bias than predictive cross-validation on the same data. Compare weighted marginal structural models, sequentially doubly robust estimators, longitudinal targeted learning and Bayesian g-computation under deliberate misspecification of each nuisance component in turn. Cross-fit at the patient level rather than the record level, and report the empirical standard-error ratio and convergence failures with the bias, since an estimator that fails to converge on a fifth of replicates is not competitive at any bias.

## Verification

::: {.verification-trail}
**Verdict.** Partially addressed. Part of this problem is addressed by existing work; the entry names which part.

**The source said.** "Marginal structural models, the parametric g-formula, g-estimation and longitudinal targeted learning all identify sustained-regime effects under sequential exchangeability and positivity, and all of them require nuisance models for treatment, censoring and outcome. When those nuisance models are fitted by machine learning, the model that predicts treatment best is not the model that produces the best causal estimate: a highly adaptive learner can achieve excellent discrimination while returning near-zero treatment probabilities, poor longitudinal balance and invalid inference. Standard cross-validation selects on prediction loss and is blind to all three. No selection criterion in routine use combines treatment prediction with longitudinal balance, weight dispersion and an estimate of the influence-function remainder, and no default library is tuned for the causal objective rather than the predictive one."

**What was wrong with it.** Balance-based criteria for the weight model are already in use: calibrated weights fitted with SuperLearner have been implemented and applied to longitudinal cohorts, so the claim that no selection criterion departs from prediction was too strong. The identification requirements also include consistency alongside sequential exchangeability and positivity, and different estimators require different nuisance components, which the entry flattened.

Literature and prior-art check
:   **partially-solved / supported-with-caveat.** The general claim, that predictive cross-validation is the wrong criterion for a nuisance model whose purpose is causal, is correct and is not new. What the entry misses is that criteria other than prediction are already in use for the weight model specifically. Calibrated weights fitted with SuperLearner have been implemented and applied to longitudinal diabetes cohorts, and calibration is precisely a balance criterion rather than a prediction criterion. Super learner for weight estimation under unknown weight-model specification was studied for marginal structural models as early as 2017. So the entry's claim that no selection criterion in routine use combines prediction with balance overstates: balance-based weight fitting exists and is published. The part that survives is the combination the entry actually asks for, a single loss spanning prediction, longitudinal balance, weight dispersion and an influence-function remainder, and the absence of a default library tuned that way.
    Cites 10.1109/jbhi.2022.3175862: Fits marginal structural model weights with SuperLearner under a calibration criterion rather than a prediction criterion, in a longitudinal EHR setting with dynamic regimes..
    Cites 10.1002/sim.7266: Studies super learner for the weight model specifically, which is the nuisance component the entry says selection is blind for..
    Cites 10.1002/sim.9568: Treats cross-validation for dynamic treatment regimes directly, in the presence of competing risks..

GPT-5.6 Sol, technical and source-code lens
:   **open / overstated.** The estimator-selection question is coherent, but the methodological setup is incorrect. Identification follows from the observed-data law plus consistency, sequential exchangeability, positivity and a well-defined intervention; estimators do not themselves identify effects. The methods listed do not all require treatment, censoring and outcome nuisance models. An IP-weighted MSM generally models treatment and censoring mechanisms; the parametric g-formula models the conditional evolution of covariates and outcomes without requiring a treatment model; standard g-estimation combines a structural model with a treatment model; longitudinal TMLE uses sequential outcome regressions and treatment or censoring mechanisms. Prediction-optimal tuning need not minimize causal error, but near-zero probabilities can reflect the true treatment process and practical positivity rather than excessive adaptivity. Predictive cross-validation does not optimize balance or weight dispersion, although those quantities are functions of its predictions and can be assessed separately. An influence-function remainder is not generally observable because it depends on unknown nuisance errors. The assertion that no routine criterion exists is a literature-coverage claim outside this audit. The ltmle capability claim is unverified because calibration.json pins only TrialEmulation and no ltmle source is vendored under documentation/refs/packages/.

Grok 4.5, recency lens
:   **open / supported.** Inverted-prior search did not find a routine selection criterion that jointly optimizes treatment prediction, longitudinal balance, weight dispersion, and an influence-function remainder for longitudinal nuisance models. SuperLearner (as used by ltmle and related stacks) still cross-validates predictive risk; CV-TMLE and related work improve targeting of the final parameter after nuisance fitting but do not replace predictive CV for the treatment, censoring, and outcome libraries themselves. Collaborative TMLE (C-TMLE) is the closest prior art: it selects confounder models using a targeted, collaborative criterion rather than pure prediction, and longitudinal/scalable C-TMLE variants exist. That is covariate-and-collaborative selection for TMLE, not a multi-metric SuperLearner loss for sustained-regime MSM, g-formula, g-estimation, or LTMLE libraries. Point-treatment work on balance-versus-discrimination for propensity scores (for example Diaz on balancing criteria) does not cover sequential longitudinal nuisance selection. Package surfaces checked in search (ltmle SuperLearner interface, SuperLearner defaults, SAS SUPERLEARNER 2024/2025) still select on predictive CV. No 2024 to 2026 AJE/Epidemiology/SiM-style paper or CRAN default library was found that implements the combined causal objective the problem names. Searches included: causal cross-validation SuperLearner longitudinal TMLE balance weight dispersion; causal loss OR targeted cross-validation nuisance MSM; collaborative TMLE longitudinal SuperLearner; propensity SuperLearner balance loss 2023 to 2026.

glm
:   **open / supported.** The claim is internally consistent and well-scoped. It asserts that no selection criterion in routine use combines treatment prediction with longitudinal balance, weight dispersion, and an influence-function remainder—this is a claim about current practice, not about impossibility. The reason given for openness is structural: the causal loss (counterfactual contrast) is never observed, so there is no label to cross-validate against, and computable surrogates like balance are not proper decision-theoretic losses. This genuinely supports the problem being open. The one sentence about no default library being tuned for the causal objective touches on software, but the core claim is methodological. The severity is proportionate: a wrong default selection criterion would propagate bias into every downstream causal estimate.

Decision path
:   `R3:partially-solved(n=1/4) → R9:substantiated-overstatement(n=1/4):codex`

:::
